title: Why he left
hookLine: he left the woods because he had several more lives to live (Walden 18)

lines: HE BUILT IT. HE LOVED IT.
cards: Why would anyone walk away from the place he wrote a whole book loving? He built the cabin with his own hands. He sounded the pond through the ice.
The bean rows, the loon, the ant war, the thaw. Then he packed up and went back to town. Readers still ask: if the woods were so good, why leave?
Thoreau saw the question coming, and in his last chapter he answers in two plain sentences that sound less like an apology than a doorway.

teach.h: AS GOOD A REASON AS I WENT.
teach.b: "I left the woods for as good a reason as I went there. Perhaps it seemed to me that I had several more lives to live, and could not spare any more time for that one." First, as good a reason.
Back in year one, this path met the reason he gave near the start of the book: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately." So leaving gets the same respect as going.
Not a failure or a retreat; the same deliberate choice, pointed the other way.
Second, several more lives. Not one life with a detour at a pond, but several, one after another, and Walden was one. That's a roomy way to see a lifetime: chapters that are each whole.
It's remarkable, Thoreau says, how easily and quietly we fall into a route and "make a beaten track for ourselves." Before long his own feet had worn a path from his door down to the water.
Even in a life chosen on purpose, a groove forms, and a groove can become a rut. Fourth, what he leaves out. Nothing says the cabin had gone stale or the experiment had failed.

teach.h: NO MORE TIME FOR THAT ONE.
teach.b: He could not spare more time for that one life, because others were waiting. The pond didn't fail him. He just had more lives to get to.

how: Readers often take Thoreau's reason for leaving Walden as permission to close a good chapter on purpose, before it hardens into habit, and to treat a life as several lives in turn.

games.q: you've lived by the pond on purpose and it's been good. a path is wearing into the ground from your door. what does Thoreau do?
o: leave, because he has several more lives to live.
games.why: he left the woods for as good a reason as he went there, and couldn't spare more time for that one life.

practice: Let one part of your life come to mind that has quietly finished, or is ready to: a habit, a role, a worry you've walked so often it's worn a path.
Don't judge it; thank it for what it gave you, and in your own words tell it this chapter is over. Notice the space it leaves, without needing to know what comes next.
